dhpak1.4:1.1: 1.3 The Story about the Elder Thulla Tissa Thullatissattheravatthu
dhpak1.4:2.1: “He abused me, he struck at me,”
dhpak1.4:2.2: [28.166] {1.37} this Dhamma teaching was given by the Teacher while he was in residence at Jetavana with reference to Elder Tissa.
dhpak1.4:3.1: It seems that this venerable elder was the son of the sister of the father of the Fortunate One.
dhpak1.4:3.2: He was an old man when he went forth, and very fat.
dhpak1.4:3.3: He enjoyed the gain and honor of the Buddhas; his clothes were always smooth from constant beating;
dhpak1.4:3.4: he always sat in the center of the monastery in the attendance hall.
dhpak1.4:4.1: One day some visiting bhikkhus came to see the Realised One, and supposing Tissa to be some great elder,
dhpak1.4:4.2: asked to be allowed the privilege of waiting upon him, offering among other things to rub his feet.
dhpak1.4:4.3: Tissa remained silent. Thereupon a certain young bhikkhu asked him: “How many Rains have you kept residence?”
dhpak1.4:4.4: – “No Rains at all,” replied Tissa, “I was an old man when I went forth.”
dhpak1.4:4.5: Said the young bhikkhu: “You wretched old bhikkhu, {1.38} you overestimate your own importance.
dhpak1.4:4.6: Seeing before you, as you do, all these great elders, you are not even civil to them.
dhpak1.4:4.7: To their offers to perform various services for you, you answer by silence.
dhpak1.4:4.8: Moreover, you show not the slightest regret for your misconduct.” So saying, he snapped his fingers.
dhpak1.4:4.9: Recovering the pride of a member of the warrior caste, Tissa asked them: “Whom did you come to see?”
dhpak1.4:4.10: – “We came to see the Teacher.” – “But with reference to me, you say to yourselves: ‘Who is he?’
dhpak1.4:4.11: I will extirpate your whole race.” So saying, he went to the Teacher, weeping and sad and sorrowful.
dhpak1.4:5.1: The Teacher asked him: “Tissa, how is it that you come to me sad and sorrowful, with tears in your eyes, weeping?”
dhpak1.4:5.2: The bhikkhus said to themselves: “If he goes alone, he may cause some trouble.”
dhpak1.4:5.3: So they went right with him, worshipped the Teacher, and sat down respectfully on one side.
dhpak1.4:5.4: Tissa answered the Teacher’s question as follows: “Venerable Sir, these bhikkhus are abusing me.”
dhpak1.4:5.5: – “But where were you sitting?” – “In the center of the monastery in the attendance hall, venerable Sir.”
dhpak1.4:5.6: – “Did you see these bhikkhus when they came?” – “Yes, venerable Sir, I saw them.”
dhpak1.4:5.7: – “Did you rise and go to meet them?” – “No, venerable Sir, I did not.”
dhpak1.4:5.8: – “Did you offer to take their monastic utensils?” – “No, venerable Sir, I did not offer to take them.”
dhpak1.4:5.9: [28.167] – “Did you offer to wait upon them and to provide them with water to drink?”
dhpak1.4:5.10: – “No, venerable Sir, I did not offer to do either of these things.” – “Did you bring seats for them and rub their feet?”
dhpak1.4:5.11: – “I did not, venerable Sir.” – “Tissa, you should have performed all these services for the senior bhikkhus,
dhpak1.4:5.12: for he who does not do this has no right to sit in the center of the monastery. You alone are to blame; ask pardon of these bhikkhus.”
dhpak1.4:5.13: – “But they {1.39} abused me, venerable Sir; I will not ask their pardon.” – “Tissa, do not act thus.
dhpak1.4:5.14: You alone are to blame; ask their pardon.” – “I will not ask their pardon, venerable Sir.”
dhpak1.4:6.1: The bhikkhus said to the Teacher: “He is an obstinate bhikkhu, venerable Sir.”
dhpak1.4:6.2: The Teacher replied: “Bhikkhus, this is not the first time he has proved obstinate;
dhpak1.4:6.3: he was obstinate also in a previous state of existence.”
dhpak1.4:6.4: – “We know all about his present obstinacy, venerable Sir; but what did he do in a previous state of existence?”
dhpak1.4:6.5: – “Well then, bhikkhus, listen,” said the Teacher. So saying, he told the following:
dhpak1.4:7.1: 3a Story of the Past: Devala and Nārada
dhpak1.4:8.1: Once upon a time, when a certain king of Bārāṇasī reigned at Bārāṇasī, an ascetic named Devala, who had resided for eight months in the Himālaya country,
dhpak1.4:8.2: desiring to reside near the city during the four months of the rains, returned from the Himālaya for salt and vinegar.
dhpak1.4:8.3: Seeing two boys at the gate of the city, he asked them: “Where do ascetics who come to this city spend the night?”
dhpak1.4:8.5: So Devala went to the potter’s hall, stopped at the door, and said:
dhpak1.4:8.6: “If it is agreeable to you, Bhaggava, I should like to spend one night in your hall.”
dhpak1.4:8.7: The potter turned over the hall to him, saying: “I have no work going on in the hall at night, and the hall is a large one;
dhpak1.4:8.8: spend the night here as you please, venerable Sir,”
dhpak1.4:9.1: Past and Present No sooner had Devala entered the hall and sat down than another ascetic named Nārada,
dhpak1.4:9.2: returning from the Himālaya, asked the potter for a night’s lodging.
dhpak1.4:9.3: The potter thought to himself: “The ascetic who arrived first may or may not be willing to spend the night with him;
dhpak1.4:9.4: I will therefore relieve myself of responsibility.”
dhpak1.4:9.5: {1.40} So he said to the ascetic who had just arrived:
dhpak1.4:9.6: “Venerable Sir, if the ascetic who arrived first approves, spend the night at his pleasure.”
dhpak1.4:9.7: So Nārada approached Devala and said: “Teacher, if it is agreeable to you, I should like to spend one night here.”
dhpak1.4:9.8: Devala replied: “The hall is a large one; therefore come in and spend the night on one side.”
dhpak1.4:9.9: So [28.168] Nārada went in and sat down behind the ascetic who had gone in before him. Both exchanged friendly greetings.
dhpak1.4:10.1: When it was bedtime, Nārada noted carefully the place where Devala lay and the position of the door, and then lay down.
dhpak1.4:10.2: But when Devala lay down, instead of lying down in his proper place, he lay down directly across the doorway.
dhpak1.4:10.3: The result was that when Nārada went out at night, he trod on Devala’s matted locks.
dhpak1.4:10.4: Thereupon Devala cried out: “Who is treading on my locks?” Nārada replied: “Teacher, it is I.”
dhpak1.4:10.5: – “False ascetic,” said Devala, “you come from the forest and tread on my locks.”
dhpak1.4:10.6: – “Teacher, I did not know that you were lying here; pardon me.”
dhpak1.4:10.7: Nārada then went out, leaving Devala weeping as if his heart would break.
dhpak1.4:11.1: Devala thought to himself: “I will let him tread on me when he comes in also.”
dhpak1.4:11.2: So he turned around and lay down, placing his head where his feet had been before.
dhpak1.4:11.3: When Nārada came in, he thought to himself: “The first time I injured the teacher; this time I will go in past his feet.”
dhpak1.4:11.4: The result was that, when Nārada entered, he trod on Devala’s neck.
dhpak1.4:11.5: Thereupon Devala cried out: “Who is that?” Nārada replied: “It is I, teacher.”
dhpak1.4:11.6: – “False ascetic,” said Devala, “the first time you trod on my locks; this time you tread on my neck.
dhpak1.4:11.7: I will curse you.” – “Teacher, I am not to blame. I did not know that you were lying in this position.
dhpak1.4:11.8: When I came in I thought to myself: ‘The first time I injured the teacher; this time I will go in past his feet.’
dhpak1.4:11.9: Pardon me.” {1.41} “False ascetic, I will curse you.” – “Do not so, teacher.”
dhpak1.4:11.10: But Devala, paying no attention to what Nārada said, cursed him all the same, saying:
dhpak1.4:12.1: A thousand rays, a hundred flames, the sun will dispel the darkness,
dhpak1.4:12.2: when the sun rises in morning, may your head split into seven.
dhpak1.4:13.1: Nārada said: “Teacher, I told you it was not my fault. But in spite of what I said, you have cursed me.
dhpak1.4:13.2: Let the head of the guilty man split into seven pieces, not that of the innocent.”
dhpak1.4:13.3: Thereupon Nārada pronounced the following curse:
dhpak1.4:14.1: A thousand rays, a hundred flames, the sun will dispel the darkness,
dhpak1.4:14.2: when the sun rises in morning, may your head split into seven.
dhpak1.4:15.1: Now Nārada possessed great supernatural power and could call to mind eighty aeons of time, forty aeons in the past and forty in the future.
dhpak1.4:15.2: So considering: “On whom will the curse fall?”
dhpak1.4:15.3: and perceiving that it would fall on his fellow-ascetic, he felt compassion for him,
dhpak1.4:15.4: and [28.169] therefore put forth his psychic power and prevented the sun from rising.
dhpak1.4:16.1: The Sun Fails to Rise When the sun failed to rise, the citizens assembled before the gate of the king’s palace and wailed:
dhpak1.4:16.2: “Your majesty, the sun has not risen, and you are king. Make the sun rise for us.”
dhpak1.4:16.3: The king surveyed his own deeds, words, and thoughts, and seeing no impropriety, thought to himself: “What can be the cause?”
dhpak1.4:16.4: Suspecting that it might be because of a quarrel of the ascetics, he enquired:
dhpak1.4:16.5: “Are there any ascetics in this city?”
dhpak1.4:16.6: – “Your majesty, last evening there were some arrivals at the potter’s hall.”
dhpak1.4:16.7: {1.42} The king immediately went there with torches carried before him, worshipped Nārada, seated himself respectfully on one side, and said:
dhpak1.4:17.1: Livelihood cannot be pursued, in Jambudīpa, Nārada,
dhpak1.4:17.2: why has the world become darkened? Answer me this when you are asked.
dhpak1.4:18.1: Nārada told him the whole story. “For this reason,” said he: “I was cursed by this ascetic.
dhpak1.4:18.2: So I cursed him back, saying: ‘I am not to blame; let the curse fall upon whichever of us is to blame.’
dhpak1.4:18.3: But when I had cursed him, I considered within myself: ‘Upon whom will the curse fall?’
dhpak1.4:18.4: and perceived that, as soon as the sun rose, the head of my fellow-ascetic would split into seven pieces.
dhpak1.4:18.5: Therefore, out of pity for him, I am not permitting the sun to rise.”
dhpak1.4:18.6: – “But, venerable Sir, how can he escape destruction?” – “He may escape destruction by begging my pardon.”
dhpak1.4:19.1: “Well then,” said the king to Devala, “beg his pardon.”
dhpak1.4:19.2: Devala replied: “Great king, this fellow trod on my matted locks and on my neck; I will not beg pardon of this false ascetic.”
dhpak1.4:19.3: – “Beg his pardon, venerable Sir; do not act thus.” – “Great king, I will not beg his pardon.”
dhpak1.4:19.4: – “Your head will split into seven pieces.” – “Nevertheless I will not beg his pardon.”
dhpak1.4:19.5: – “I am convinced that you will not beg his pardon of your own free will,” said the king.
dhpak1.4:20.1: Thereupon, taking him by the hands, feet, belly, and neck, the king compelled him to bow down before Nārada’s feet.
dhpak1.4:20.2: Nārada said: “Rise, teacher, I pardon you.”
dhpak1.4:20.3: Then said Nārada to the king: “Great king, since this ascetic does not ask pardon of his own free will,
dhpak1.4:20.4: {1.43} take him to a certain lake not far from the city,
dhpak1.4:20.5: put a lump of clay on top of his head, and make him stand in the water up to his neck.”
dhpak1.4:21.1: The king did so. Then said Nārada to Devala: “Teacher, I will put forth my psychic power and cause the sun to rise.
dhpak1.4:21.2: At that moment [28.170] duck in the water, rise in a different place, and go your way.”
dhpak1.4:21.3: As soon as the sun’s rays touched the lump of clay, it split into seven pieces.
dhpak1.4:21.4: Thereupon Devala ducked in the water, rose in a different place, and ran away.
dhpak1.4:22.1: When the Teacher had given this Dhamma teaching, he said:
dhpak1.4:22.2: “Bhikkhus, at that time the king was Ānanda, Devala was Tissa, and Nārada was I myself; at that time also he was obstinate.”
dhpak1.4:23.1: Then he addressed the Elder Tissa as follows: “Tissa, if a bhikkhu allows himself to think: ‘So and so abused me.
dhpak1.4:23.2: So and so struck me. So and so defeated me. So and so robbed me of my goods,’ his hatred never ceases.
dhpak1.4:23.3: But if he does not cherish such thoughts, his hatred ceases.”
dhpak1.4:23.4: So saying, he pronounced the following verses:
dhpak1.4:24.1: 3. “Akkocchi maṁ, avadhi maṁ, ajini maṁ, ahāsi me”,
dhpak1.4:24.2: ye ca taṁ upanayhanti, veraṁ tesaṁ na sammati.
dhpak1.4:25.1: “He abused me, he struck at me, he overcame me, he robbed me,”
dhpak1.4:25.2: those who bear ill-will towards this, their hatred is never appeased.
dhpak1.4:26.1: 4. “Akkocchi maṁ, avadhi maṁ, ajini maṁ, ahāsi me”,
dhpak1.4:26.2: ye taṁ na upanayhanti, veraṁ tesūpasammati.
dhpak1.4:27.1: “He abused me, he struck at me, he overcame me, he robbed me,”
dhpak1.4:27.2: those who bear not ill-will towards this, their hatred is surely appeased.
dhpak1.4:28.1: At the end of the verse 100,000 bhikkhus attained the fruition of Stream-entry.
dhpak1.4:28.2: The teaching of the Dhamma was of benefit to many people.
dhpak1.4:28.3: Such is the one hard to speak to, and the one easy to speak to.
